title: Short Stuff: The History of Paternity Testing
summary: Short Stuff episode on the history of paternity testing. The hosts open with the legend of Saint Anthony, who supposedly had a baby identify its father, then move to pseudoscientific methods of the early 20th century: examining the roof of the mouth for ridges, eugenics-style measurements of nose, ears and hair, and Dr. Albert Abrams' oscillophore, which claimed blood vibrations revealed ethnic heritage. Judge Thomas Graham Taft... (see segments) used Abrams' test in a San Francisco case involving Paul Vittori, a result the hosts call a gross miscarriage of justice. Blood typing then gave the first scientific basis for ruling men in or out, and it became public in the Charlie Chaplin paternity case brought by Joan Barry, where the jury still ruled Chaplin the legal father. California in 1953 made scientific exclusion results binding, other states followed, and genetic DNA testing eventually replaced blood typing. The episode ends with cheap home tests versus lab fees and a mention of Maury Povich's paternity reveals and a Dave Rouse article on HowStuffWorks.

entities.name: Paternity: The Elusive Quest for the Father

segments.title: Opening and Saint Anthony legend
segments.summary: Josh introduces paternity testing history and recounts the legend of Saint Anthony, in which an infant supposedly named its father to clear a wife accused of infidelity. The hosts mention Nara Milanich's book and Dave Rouse's article.

segments.title: Early pseudoscientific paternity methods
segments.summary: Before reliable science, quacks filled the gap. Examples include claims that roof-of-the-mouth ridges were inherited like fingerprints, eugenics-style measurements of nose, ears and hair, and a 1920s panic over switched babies in hospitals.

segments.title: Albert Abrams and the oscillophore
segments.summary: Dr. Albert Abrams claimed his oscillophore could measure blood vibrations linked to ethnic heritage. Judge Thomas Graham used this method in a San Francisco case against Paul Vittori, who was ruled the father despite denying it.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Sponsor break before the segment on blood typing.

segments.title: Blood typing and the Charlie Chaplin case
segments.summary: Discovery of blood types gave the first scientific way to narrow down a possible father. Joan Barry sued Charlie Chaplin; science showed he was not the biological father, but the jury still found him liable for support because of his relationship with her.

segments.title: Legal changes and modern testing
segments.summary: California in 1953 made scientific exclusion binding, and other states followed. Genetic testing replaced blood typing in the 1980s and 1990s. Home tests are cheap, but lab fees make the total over a hundred dollars, and drugstore tests cannot give results.

segments.title: Pop culture aside and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts mention Maury Povich's on-air paternity reveals, point listeners to Dave Rouse's HowStuffWorks article, and sign off.
